creator: Dunne & Raby with Michael Anastassiades
quote: What would have to change for a need like this to emerge?
description: The clock in Do You Want to Replace the Existing Normal? reports fatalities by transport category. The authors imagine demand for an everyday object that reminds people of mortality. The question concerns the values and needs of that world, not a novel clock display.
gap: The current task offers AI answers, but no different museum arrangement. Checking accuracy alone investigates information use rather than a speculative alternative.
world: An imagined museum gives the AI’s first interpretation default visibility. A visitor’s alternative can challenge it, but must be deliberately retained.
prop: After the ordinary task, show a clearly fictional first-interpretation record with the AI version marked as the default. Ask what a museum would have to value for this rule to make sense and whether the visitor would keep it.
tension: Convenient orientation versus the visitor’s freedom to set the interpretive starting point.
selection: Keep 1 as an introduction. An authority-focused revision is possible, but it adds a separate question and is not needed for the first A/B trial.
limit: The clock is an analogy for questioning a need or default. It does not prove that AI-first museum interpretation is harmful or unprecedented.

creator: Charles Avery, discussed by Dunne & Raby
quote: It is the emphasis on transporting the imagination that distinguishes them from other object types including products, prototypes, and models.
description: The book describes drawings, objects, models and found bones attributed to a fictional traveller’s observations of an imaginary island. A small object invites viewers to imagine the wider world it belongs to. It is not simply an unusual object to own.
gap: Handling cloth, using AI and printing a card are still ordinary activity features. None by itself changes the arrangement through which a visit is represented.
world: An imagined museum treats the AI-written card as the default lasting record of the visitor’s making. The visitor must decide whose account should represent that experience.
prop: Use the existing card, clearly labelled as a future-scenario prop, and ask which account would remain if only one were carried forward. The visitor may keep AI wording, replace it or reject the rule.
tension: An orderly institutional record versus first-person authority over lived experience.
selection: Prioritize A conditionally. The same card already produced by the activity can make a broader recording rule discussable with little extra effort. The speculative question concerns representation, not whether the cloth becomes historical.
limit: The Islanders informs how a small prop can suggest a world. It does not validate an AI card or show that visitors will interpret the scenario as intended.

creator: Troika, discussed by Dunne & Raby
quote: There is a very important difference between inviting viewers to “make-believe” and asking them to “believe.”
description: Troika’s fictitious plants combine plausible-looking images with short accounts of their roles in a near-future London. The project signals fiction while making a specific environmental arrangement imaginable. It is not presented as a factual plant discovery.
gap: Changing a colour or outline supplies a visual alternative, but does not yet identify which heritage value or interpretive arrangement is at stake.
world: A possible later version imagines a museum that adapts a pattern according to a stated contemporary priority. A short fictional label identifies that priority and what the adaptation leaves behind.
prop: Compare the approved source and one clearly labelled imagined adaptation. Ask what should remain recognisable and why. Keep historical facts separate, and do not describe the variant as a restoration.
tension: Contemporary reuse versus continuity with a source, its context and its meaning.
selection: Pause the standalone probe. First specify a meaningful adaptation and its contextual stakes. More attractive editing or a printed card does not resolve this gap.
limit: Plant Fiction supports framing and legibility of the fiction. It does not make an arbitrary image edit speculative, historically defensible or ethically appropriate.

creator: Dunne & Raby
quote: Each vehicle would embody different ideologies, values, priorities, and belief systems—essentially alternative worldviews.
description: Different vehicles make alternative arrangements of everyday life and their trade-offs available for comparison. The comparison works because the objects embody different priorities. Four unusual vehicle designs alone would not communicate that argument.
gap: Two languages or two opinions are not yet a different institutional arrangement. A jointly written label may even hide the disagreement the probe needs to investigate.
world: After a real exchange, imagine that a museum shows the AI translation as the public default while filing the originals separately. Visitors consider who may authorize that visibility rule.
prop: Use one existing conversation card plus a fictional display-rule strip. Participants can keep the default, require original and translation together, or refuse the proposed rule. These are discussion choices, not implemented publishing permissions.
tension: Cross-language readability versus control over which voices and differences remain visible.
selection: Merge with 5 as B. 4 supplies the public interpretation question, while 5 adds a real recipient and a chance to correct understanding. A stated visibility rule gives the merged activity a more concrete speculative focus.
limit: A difference of language is not a proxy for one of the book’s political systems. The transferable principle is making priorities and trade-offs visible, not classifying visitors into cultural types.

creator: Dunne & Raby with Michael Anastassiades
quote: It is through its demeanor that one starts to wonder just how serious it is.
description: The soft, huggable mushroom forms refer to nuclear tests. The book describes a tension between their inviting material presence and what they represent. Their critical force is not equivalent to being cute, soft or amusing.
gap: Gifting or making a message warmer is not automatically speculative. Optional emoji can make an exchange pleasant without raising a question about what that representation retains or changes.
world: Within B’s imagined museum arrangement, an AI bridge message may make another person’s account easier or friendlier to read. Ask who can authorize that reframing when it changes hesitation, tone or a difficult personal association.
prop: Keep the original wording, AI wording and a real recipient’s reply on the same card. Discuss a meaningful difference and whether a future museum may retain the reworded version as the default. Do not require a disagreement or introduce a misleading historical claim.
tension: Ease and warmth of communication versus fidelity to the sender’s tone and the object’s context.
selection: Merge with 4. The real recipient makes a representation’s consequence discussable. Keep generated expressions as a later branch, rather than treating visual play as the source of speculation.
limit: The book’s deliberately conflicting material form is a methodological analogy. It is not evidence that emoji communicate universally or that heritage messages should be made shocking.
